title: Latency buckets
text: An LLM request can be broken into client overhead, network transfer, prompt tokenization or prefill, token generation, and local post-processing. Local backends often expose prompt evaluation and generation durations, while hosted APIs usually expose only wall time and token usage.

title: Energy measurement
text: CPU energy can sometimes be read from Linux RAPL counters. NVIDIA GPU power can be sampled through NVML. If direct CPU package energy is unavailable, utilization multiplied by a configured TDP can be used as a rough estimate, but it should be labeled as an estimate.

title: Cost per request
text: Cost per request combines provider token charges, optional hardware amortization, and electricity. For hosted APIs, input and output tokens often have different prices. For local inference, token charges are zero but electricity and hardware capacity still matter.

title: Batching embeddings
text: Embedding workloads often benefit from batching because network overhead and model setup costs are shared across many inputs. The best batch size depends on memory, endpoint limits, and the shape of the input texts.

title: RAG query pipeline
text: A simple RAG query embeds the user question, ranks corpus chunks by vector similarity, selects the top results, and optionally sends the selected context to a generation model. Ranking time is usually small for tiny corpora and grows with corpus size.

title: CPU versus GPU
text: Running the same local model on CPU and GPU can change latency, throughput, and energy. A GPU may use more instantaneous power but finish sooner, so total energy must be measured rather than inferred from watts alone.

title: Summarization workload
text: Document summarization is dominated by input tokens when documents are long. Output length controls generation time, while chunking strategy and context length determine how many requests are needed.

title: Classification workload
text: Classification prompts usually have short outputs. Their cost and latency are often dominated by prompt length, label instructions, network overhead, and any schema validation or parsing performed after the response.
